extracted.intended_audience: general readers and fans of comedy/performance art
extracted.subtask_description: A Wikipedia biographical article describing Andy Kaufman's life, career, distinctive comedic style, notable performances, and legacy. The page documents examples and incidents that illustrate his approach to performance art and comedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Style (performance genres listed)
rubrics_metrics.description: Style: Alternative comedy; Anti-humor; cringe humor; character comedy; surreal comedy; improvisational comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These style labels (from the article infobox) identify the genres and registers Kaufman's work is associated with and frame how his performances should be understood and evaluated — i.e., not as conventional joke-telling but as character-driven, surreal, or deliberately awkward performances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-comedian / refusal of traditional joke-telling
rubrics_metrics.description: He disdained telling jokes and engaging in comedy as it was traditionally understood, once saying, 'I am not a comic, I have never told a joke. The comedian's promise is that he will go out there and make you laugh with him. My only promise is that I will try to entertain you as best I can.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kaufman's approach should be judged by whether it entertains or provokes in nontraditional ways rather than by conventional joke structure or punchline delivery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of recurring characters and persona work / blurring performer-character boundary
rubrics_metrics.description: Kaufman frequently performed as characters (e.g., Foreign Man/Latka Gravas and Tony Clifton), sometimes appearing as himself and sometimes as obnoxiously rude lounge singer Tony Clifton; at times it was unclear to audiences who Clifton actually was.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation of his work often focuses on the effectiveness of sustained personas and the deliberate ambiguity between the actor and the character (including presenting a character as a 'real person'), and the extent to which that blurring contributes to the performance's artistic goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of pranks, elaborate ruses, and staged hoaxes
rubrics_metrics.description: As pranks and elaborate ruses were major elements of his career; examples include staged incidents (fake heart attack onstage, staged fights, running hoaxes such as the long-running Tony Clifton ruse, and persistent rumors that Kaufman faked his own death).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A central criterion is how deliberately the performer uses hoaxes and ruses to shape audience reaction and meaning; effectiveness is measured by the extent to which the ruse reshapes audience expectations and conversation rather than straightforwardly 'deceiving' without artistic purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Willingness to provoke negative or confused audience reactions
rubrics_metrics.description: He is respected for his willingness to provoke negative and confused reactions from audiences; this includes routines that angered or alienated viewers (e.g., the female-wrestling routine on SNL which prompted a phone vote to 'Dump Andy').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kaufman's work is often evaluated by whether it successfully engenders discomfort, puzzlement, or antagonism as an artistic strategy, rather than by audience-laughter-as-success alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meta-gags and staging that rely on audience misunderstanding
rubrics_metrics.description: He used meta-humor and staging that could be mistaken for technical or social error (e.g., a segment with fake television screen static intended to look like broadcast problems; breaking the fourth wall and simulated 'apologies' on live shows).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A useful criterion is whether the meta-element reliably manipulates audience framing — leveraging confusion, interruption, or perceived malfunction to make a comic/performative point — and how clearly/ambiguously that manipulation is signaled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Immersive and extended showmanship beyond conventional set pieces
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples include his Carnegie Hall show where he staged a 'grandmother' reveal (Robin Williams) and an onstage 'death' revival, then took the entire audience in buses for milk and cookies and continued the show on the Staten Island Ferry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether performances extend beyond a discrete club set into immersive, time-extended experiences that alter the audience's role and expectations, and whether that extension serves a coherent artistic aim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incorporation of theatrical kayfabe and sporting spectacle (professional wrestling)
rubrics_metrics.description: Kaufman incorporated professional wrestling's theatricality and kayfabe into his act (wrestling women, proclaiming himself 'Inter-Gender Wrestling Champion,' staging feuds such as with Jerry 'The King' Lawler, and offering prizes), treating wrestling as performance art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessments should consider how effectively the performer borrows from 'staged' sporting traditions to create a hybrid of theatrical spectacle and comedy, and how the deliberate use of kayfabe contributes to meaning and audience reaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contractual / production requirement: treating a character as a real person
rubrics_metrics.description: As a requirement for Kaufman's accepting the offer to star on Taxi, he insisted that Clifton be hired for a guest role on the show 'as if he were a real person, not a character.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This documents an explicit production/contractual standard: when integrating a persona into mainstream media, the performer may demand that production present the persona as real — a requirement that shapes how the performance is framed for broader audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legacy / evaluative criteria for the Andy Kaufman Award
rubrics_metrics.description: The Andy Kaufman Award is 'a showcase for promising cutting-edge artists with fresh and unconventional material, for those willing to take risks with an audience, and for those who do not define themselves by the typical conventions of comedy.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an explicit, posthumous evaluative rubric: entrants are judged on originality, unconventionality, risk-taking with live audiences, and refusal to follow typical comedy conventions.
